Reading Hair and Scalp Before Every Service

Every safe service starts before the first part is made. In this module you learn a five-minute hands-on hair assessment, a scalp check that tells you when to serve, postpone or refer, and a written consultation that matches the style to the hair in front of you.

A client sits down and says, "I want small knotless braids, waist length." A beginner starts parting. A professional first spends about five minutes looking at the hair, because the same style can be safe on one head and harmful on another. This lesson gives you four simple checks that need nothing more than your hands, a tail comb, a spray bottle of clean water, a strand of sewing thread and good light.

Look closely before you agree to any style: four quick checks guide every decision in this course.
Check 1: density (how much hair there is)

Density means how many strands grow on each part of the scalp. It is not the same as how thick each strand is. To test it, make a straight part at the crown on dry hair and look at how much scalp you can see. If the scalp is hard to see, density is high. If you see a clear line of scalp, it is medium. If the scalp shows easily even before you part, density is low. Repeat at the front hairline, the temples and the nape, because density is rarely the same everywhere. The temples and edges are often the thinnest part of the head, and they are also the part that suffers most from tight styling.
Check 2: strand width (fine, medium or coarse)

Pick up one shed strand from her comb or shoulders. Hold it next to a piece of ordinary sewing thread. If the hair looks thinner than the thread and you can hardly feel it when you roll it between finger and thumb, it is fine. If it is about the same, it is medium. If it feels wiry and thicker than the thread, it is coarse. Fine strands break more easily under tension and heat, so a client with fine hair needs gentler handling and less added weight, even if she has plenty of hair.
Check 3: porosity (how hair takes in and loses water)

Porosity describes how easily water gets into the strand and how quickly it leaves again. It depends on the cuticle, the outer layer of overlapping scales. You observe it during the wash rather than guessing. Spray a small clean section with water. If the water sits in droplets on top and the hair takes a long time to get wet and a long time to dry, porosity is low. If the hair soaks up water at once, dries quickly and feels rough or frizzes, porosity is high. Ends that have been coloured, relaxed or heated often behave differently from the roots, so test both.
Check 4: elasticity (how hair stretches and returns)
Take one wet strand from the back of the head, where it will not be missed.
Hold it firmly near the root with one hand so you do not pull the scalp.
With the other hand, stretch the strand slowly and gently, then release.

Healthy hair stretches a little and springs back. Hair that snaps almost at once is dry and brittle. Hair that stretches a long way, feels gummy and stays stretched is weak and needs very gentle handling.
Write the result on her card. Never repeat the test on the same strand.

Worked example: from findings to a safer style
For example, Amaka runs a home salon in Enugu. Her client Funmi asks for small waist-length knotless braids for a wedding.

Use good light
Do the checks by a window in daylight or with a phone torch. Dim light hides thin patches at the temples and makes density look higher than it is.

Hair changes. A client who wore heavy braids for months, had a baby, changed diet or started colouring can have very different hair from her last visit. That honest note is one of the most valuable things a stylist can give a client.

Your hands touch more scalps in a month than many health workers do. That makes you an important early warning. It does not make you a doctor. Your job is to notice, to protect the client and your next clients, and to point her to the right help. You never diagnose and you never recommend or apply medicine. This lesson shows you how to look, what to look for, and what to do with what you find.

How to do the scalp check
Wash your hands and seat the client in good light, before you wet or comb the hair.
Ask: "Is any part of your scalp sore, itchy or tender? Have you had any treatment, relaxer or colour in the last two weeks?"
Using the tail of a clean comb, make parts about two finger-widths apart from the front hairline back to the nape.
Look along every part, and specially at the hairline, temples, crown, behind the ears and the nape.
If you see broken skin, sores or pus, put on disposable gloves before you touch the area again.
Write what you saw on the client card, even when everything is healthy.

Facts about head lice

According to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), head lice cannot hop or fly. They spread mainly through direct contact with the hair of a person who has lice, and also through shared combs, brushes, towels, hats and scarves. Adult lice usually die within two days off the head.
Saying it kindly and privately

Clients feel embarrassed about lice or ringworm, and mothers worry they will be blamed. Never announce what you found in front of other clients. Step aside and use calm words: "I noticed some patches on her scalp that I am not trained to judge. I don't want to braid over them and make them worse. Please let a health worker look at it first, and I will keep your booking for when she is cleared." Avoid naming a condition as a fact. Say what you saw, not what you think it is.
Cleaning tools after a problem scalp

Put every comb, clip and towel you touched into a separate bag. For lice, the CDC advises soaking combs and brushes in hot water of at least about 54°C (130°F) for 5 to 10 minutes, and washing towels and capes on a hot cycle. For a suspected fungal infection, wash tools with soap and water, then disinfect them as you will learn in Module 4. Wash your hands for a full 40 to 60 seconds afterwards.
Worked example: two sisters, one problem
For example, Halima in Kaduna has a booking to cornrow two sisters aged 7 and 9. Their mother paid a deposit of about ₦2,000 by transfer.
During the scalp check, Halima sees two round scaly patches with broken hairs on the younger girl's crown.
She stops, puts that comb and towel in a bag, and checks the older sister carefully with a fresh comb. Her scalp looks healthy.
She speaks to the mother privately, describes what she saw, and suggests the clinic before the younger girl's hair is done.
She braids the older sister with fresh tools and keeps the ₦2,000 deposit as credit for the younger girl's appointment.
After the session she washes and disinfects every tool, and writes the date and what she saw on both girls' cards.

One child is served safely, the other is referred without embarrassment, no tools carry the problem to other clients, and the family's money is kept as credit, so the mother trusts Halima and comes back.

Never recommend a medicine, give a dose, or apply any treatment to a scalp problem. Never put relaxer, colour or any chemical on broken or sore skin. Your role is to stop, protect and refer.

Estimating time before you quote

Clients want to know how long they will sit. Use your own timed average per braid or row, not a guess. Count how many sections the style needs, multiply by your minutes per section, then add the wash, drying and finishing. You will build your personal timing log in Module 4. Until then, time yourself on practice heads and use those numbers.
Worked example: a consultation that changes the plan
For example, Chioma runs a salon corner in Onitsha. A client wants small knotless braids, waist length, for a wedding in ten days.
Assessment shows medium density at the crown and thin temples. Chioma explains that waist-length small braids would hang heavily on thin edges.
They agree on medium knotless braids, mid-back length, with the temple hair braided without added hair.
Chioma counts the plan: 8 rows with an average of 10 braids per row gives 8 x 10 = 80 braids.
Her timed average for medium knotless is 6 minutes per braid: 80 x 6 = 480 minutes, which is 8 hours of braiding.

She adds 30 minutes for washing and 60 minutes for drying and stretching: 480 + 30 + 60 = 570 minutes, which is 9 hours 30 minutes in total. She writes this on the card with the agreed price and takes a deposit.
The client knows the style, size, length, time and price in advance. She chooses to come two days before the wedding, starting at 8 a.m., and nothing about the day is a surprise.
When she insists on a style her hair cannot carry

Sometimes a client hears your advice and still wants the tiny, heavy, very long braids. Explain once, calmly, what you saw: "Your temples are thinner than the rest of your hair, and this length adds a lot of weight there." Offer two safer versions of the look she likes, such as a bigger size, a shorter length, or leaving the edges out. If she still insists, you may decline that part of the service. Write on her card what you advised and what was agreed. A stylist who says no to damage keeps clients for years, because their hair stays healthy.
Children and consent

For a child, the parent or guardian agrees to the style, the time and the price, and must say whether photos may be taken. Never post a child's photo, or any client's face, without clear permission recorded on the card.

Before you start, read the key points back to her: "Medium knotless, mid-back, temples without added hair, about nine and a half hours, this price, your deposit received, no photos of your face." Ask her to reply "agreed" on WhatsApp if you booked there. That one message is your record if there is ever a dispute.

Neat, long-lasting braids start with clean, conditioned, detangled and stretched hair. This module turns washing and prepping into a timed salon service you can deliver with or without a basin, with methods that protect the hair and the client's comfort.

Many home salons in Nigeria have no backwash basin and no constant running water. That does not stop you giving a clean, comfortable, professional wash. What matters is the order of steps, the water temperature, washing in sections, and protecting the client's clothes, eyes and neck. This lesson sets up the service so it takes about 30 minutes and leaves hair ready to condition and stretch.
A bucket
Two buckets and a jug can give a clean, comfortable wash where there is no basin.
Setting up a two-bucket station
**Bucket A (clean water):** fill it with lukewarm water. Mix hot water into cold, never the other way round, and test it on the inside of your wrist. It should feel comfortably warm, not hot.
**Bucket B (used water):** placed under the client's head or beside the chair to catch rinse water.
**A jug or cup** for pouring, and a spray bottle for small sections.
**A cape or large plastic sheet**, a neck towel, and a dry towel for blotting.
**Shampoo, conditioner and a wide-tooth comb** within reach, so you never leave her with wet hair to fetch things.
**A low stool** so the client can lean forward over Bucket B, or a chair with a neck rest if she prefers to lean back.
Hot water and electricity

If you heat water with an electric kettle or immersion heater, do it away from the wash area and never with wet hands. Keep cables away from water and from the client's feet. Always mix and test water before it touches her head, and be extra careful with children.
Wash in sections

Coily hair tangles when it is rubbed loose in one big mass. Before wetting, divide the hair into four to six sections and twist or loosely band each one. You wash and rinse one section at a time while the others stay in place. The hair stays organised, tangles much less, and detangling later is faster.
The wash step by step
Seat the client, put on the cape and neck towel, and ask her to hold a small towel over her eyes.
Wet one section thoroughly with the jug, letting the water run into Bucket B.

Apply a small amount of shampoo to the scalp only. The American Academy of Dermatology (AAD) advises massaging shampoo gently into the scalp and letting it flow through the length, rather than rubbing the length.
Use the pads of your fingers, never your nails, to work along the scalp.
Rinse until the water runs clear, then twist the section back and move to the next one.
Apply conditioner to the length of each section. The AAD advises using conditioner after every shampoo.
Rinse, then wrap the hair in a towel to absorb water. Do not rub it, which the AAD lists as a damaging habit.

Common wash mistakes to avoid
**Piling all the hair on top of the head** and scrubbing it in circles. This creates knots that take longer to undo than the wash itself.
**Using too much shampoo.** A small amount on the scalp is enough; extra product is wasted money and takes longer to rinse.
**Leaving product in the hair.** Rinse each section until the water runs clear and the hair no longer feels slippery with shampoo. Leftover product can leave the scalp itchy under braids.
**Forgetting the ears and neck.** Wipe away water and foam from behind the ears and the hairline before she sits up, and change the neck towel if it is wet.
Worked example: what one wash costs
For example, Bisi runs a home salon in Ibadan and wants to know what to add to her price for a wash service. Prices here are approximate and change often.

Conditioner: a 500 ml bottle costs about ₦5,000. One wash uses about 30 ml. Cost: 30 ÷ 500 x 5,000 = ₦300.

Hair must be fully dry before braiding with extensions. Damp hair sealed inside braids dries very slowly and can become unpleasant to wear. Low-porosity hair, which you identified in Module 1, takes the longest to dry, so book extra time for it. You will learn to dry and stretch hair at the same time in the next lesson.

Tightly coiled hair shrinks as it dries. Shrunken hair is hard to part cleanly and hard to braid smoothly, so most stylists stretch the hair before braiding or twisting. You can stretch with heat or without heat. Both work. The right choice depends on the client's hair, her time and the style. This lesson also shows you how to add a deep conditioning step as a paid extra.
A bottle of hair conditioner
Conditioning before you stretch makes the hair softer, easier to part and less likely to break.
Deep conditioning in a salon service

A deep conditioner (also called a hair mask or treatment) is thicker than a rinse-out conditioner and stays on longer. After shampooing, apply it section by section from the length to the ends, cover the hair with a plastic cap, and leave it for the time written on the label. Some products say to use gentle warmth from a hooded dryer or a warm towel; others do not. Follow the label, not a guess, and never leave a product on longer than it says. Rinse with lukewarm water until the hair no longer feels slippery with product.

Blow-drying safely

The AAD advises letting hair air dry when possible and using the lowest heat setting when you do use a dryer. Apply a heat protectant to each section, keep the dryer moving, and point the air down the hair shaft from root to ends. Work on hair that is damp, not dripping, so you spend less time under heat. Stop and check the client's scalp and ears are not getting hot. If the hair smells burnt or the ends feel crispy, the heat is too high.
African threading as a stretch
On damp, conditioned hair, make a section about the width of two fingers.
Hold the section at the root and tie the end of a soft thread or wool around its base, not tight on the scalp.
Wrap the thread down the section in close spirals, keeping the hair taut but not pulling the scalp.
Stop just before the ends, tuck the thread under the last wrap, and leave the tips free.
Leave the threads in until the hair is completely dry, usually overnight, then unwind them gently.

Checking the hair is ready

Before you start braiding, test that the hair is fully dry and evenly stretched. Feel the roots at the nape and behind the ears, where hair dries last. If the roots feel cool or damp, dry that area again before parting. Look at the ends: if they are split, thin or tangled into small knots, offer to trim only the damaged tips with clean, sharp hair scissors, and only with her agreement. Smooth, even ends make neater braids and a cleaner finish.
Worked example: planning a stretch around the client's day
For example, Ngozi in Abuja has a client with fine, low-porosity hair who wants braids starting at 9 a.m. on Saturday.
Option A, all on Saturday: wash 30 minutes + deep condition 20 minutes + blow-dry 45 minutes = 95 minutes before braiding starts. Braiding begins at about 10:35 a.m.

Detangling is where most damage happens in a salon, because it is slow and stylists get impatient. Pulling a comb from the roots through a knot breaks strands and hurts the client. The professional method is the opposite: small sections, plenty of slip, start at the ends and work up, and always hold the hair so the pull never reaches the scalp.

Clients judge a braid style first by its parts. Straight, even parts make even cheap extension hair look expensive. Crooked, uneven parts make a style look rushed, and uneven sections also carry uneven weight, which strains the smaller ones. This lesson teaches the two parting patterns used for most box braids and twists, how to count braids before you start, and a quick natural-hair style, flat twists, that you can offer at a lower price.

Tools for parting

Square grid and brick-lay

In a **square grid**, every row is divided at the same points, so the parts form straight lines from front to back like a chessboard. It looks very neat when the hair is tied up, but straight channels of scalp show when braids fall loose. In a **brick-lay** pattern, each row is shifted by half a section, like bricks in a wall. The parts of one row sit behind the middle of the braids in the row above, so the scalp is covered better when the braids hang down. Brick-lay usually means one row has one braid fewer than the next.

Parting step by step
Start at the nape. Draw the first horizontal row about the height you want each section to be, and clip all hair above it away.
Divide the row into equal sections. Use your fingers or the comb's teeth as a ruler so each section is the same width.
Smooth each section with a little product so stray hairs do not cross into the next part.
Braid or twist the whole row before parting the next, so you always work from a clean line.
For brick-lay, start the next row's first part in the middle of the section below it.
After every two rows, take a phone photo from behind and check that sizes are even.

For example, Aisha in Kano plans medium box braids in brick-lay for a client and wants to quote the time.
She maps 8 rows from nape to front.

Her timed average for medium box braids is 6 minutes each: 76 x 6 = 456 minutes, which is 7 hours 36 minutes of braiding.
Aisha quotes about 7 hours 40 minutes of braiding, plus prep time, and buys extension hair for 76 braids instead of guessing.
Flat twists on natural hair

A flat twist lies flat against the scalp like a cornrow, but it uses two strands twisted over each other instead of three braided. It needs no extension hair, takes less time, and suits clients who want a lighter, cheaper style or a protective style between braid installations.
Part a straight row from the front hairline towards the nape, about two to three fingers wide. Clip the rest away.
At the front, take two small strands from the section.
Cross the right strand over the left, then pick up a little loose hair from the section and add it to the strand that is now on the right.
Repeat: cross, pick up, add, keeping the twist flat on the scalp and the tension gentle.
When the section ends, continue as a two-strand twist to the ends and coil the tip around your finger.

For example, six flat twists at about 12 minutes each take 6 x 12 = 72 minutes, a quick service you can fit between longer bookings. Clients can wear them as a style, or unravel them after a few days for a stretched twist-out.

Three parting problems cause most redos. Sections that grow bigger towards the front happen when you stop measuring with your fingers as you get tired, so check the size against the first row. Parts that drift sideways happen when the client tilts her head; ask her to keep her chin level and look straight ahead. Fuzzy parts happen on dry hair, so lightly mist and smooth each row before you draw the line.

Knotless braids are among the most requested braid styles because they look natural at the root and put less sudden weight on the scalp at the start of each braid. African threading, known in Yoruba as **irun kiko**, is one of the oldest Nigerian styling methods, using thread wrapped around sections of natural hair. One is a modern extension style; the other needs no extensions at all. Offering both widens your menu and your price range.
A knotted rope

How a knotless braid is built

In a traditional box braid, a folded piece of extension hair is looped around the base of the section, so the braid starts with added weight and a small bump of extension hair at the root. In a knotless braid, you start braiding the client's own hair alone for a few stitches, then add very small pieces of extension hair one at a time as you braid down. The root looks like her own hair, and the weight builds gradually.
Part a clean section and smooth it with a little product. Divide the section's own hair into three strands.
Braid two or three stitches with her hair only, keeping the tension firm but painless.
Lay a thin feed-in piece of extension hair, folded in half, over the braid so each half joins a side strand.
Braid two or three more stitches, then add the next feed-in piece the same way.
Continue adding pieces until the braid reaches the thickness you agreed, then braid to the end without adding more.
Run your fingers down the braid to check that no extension hair is poking out, and that the root does not tug when the client turns her head.

Prepare all your feed-in pieces before the client sits down. Pre-stretched braiding hair saves time because the ends are already tapered. Split each pack into pieces of a consistent size, roughly the same thickness each time, and lay them in labelled piles. Count the pieces you need from your braid plan, not by guesswork.

Finishing the ends safely

Many stylists dip synthetic braid ends in hot water to seal and smooth them. Hot water burns quickly. Ask the client to stand or lean away, protect her neck and shoulders with a towel, hold the cup or flask yourself well below her shoulders, and dip only the ends. Never pour hot water over braids still on her head near the skin. Synthetic hair can also catch fire, so never use a lighter or open flame near a client's head.

Keep the kettle and flask on a stable surface away from children and walkways. Water that has just boiled can scald in a second. If skin is burned, cool it under clean running water and seek medical help for anything more than a small, mild burn.
African threading (irun kiko)
On clean, stretched, moisturised hair, part the sections for the chosen design, often a crown of upright or curved threaded stems.
Use a soft black thread or wool. Tie it at the base of the section without pulling the scalp.
Wrap the thread down the section in tight, even spirals so the hair is completely covered, like a smooth cord.
Bend or join the threaded stems into the design: curves, arches, or bunches meeting at the crown.
Secure the ends by tucking the thread under the last wraps.

Threading is light because it adds no extension hair, and it stretches the hair as it holds the style. The tension risk is at the base: if the thread is tied tightly against the scalp, or if many stems are pulled to one point, the hairline is strained. Leave a little slack at the base of every section and ask the client how it feels before you move on.

Feed-in cornrows with safe tension: preventing traction alopecia
Install a feed-in cornrow that starts thin and builds gradually

Traction alopecia is hair loss caused by repeated pulling on the hair, usually from tight braids, cornrows, ponytails, weaves and extensions. It often starts at the temples and hairline, the same places where hair is thinnest. Long-term pulling can lead to permanent hair loss. As a stylist you can prevent much of it, with technique, with honesty and with the advice you give. This lesson teaches feed-in cornrows, a style where tension control is especially important.
A warning sign
Pain during braiding is a warning, not a sign the style will last longer.
Feed-in cornrows step by step
Part a clean row from the hairline towards the nape. Leave the finest baby hairs at the front out of the cornrow.
Start braiding with her own hair only for the first few stitches, using an underhand or overhand cornrow stitch.
Add a very thin piece of extension hair to a side strand, braid two or three stitches, and add another thin piece.
Keep adding thin pieces until the row reaches the agreed thickness. The row should look thin at the front and fuller at the back.
Braid off the scalp to the end of the extension hair and finish the end.

Feed-in cornrows look natural at the front because they start thin. That also protects her hairline, because the first stitches carry no extension weight. Never start a cornrow with a thick piece of added hair at the hairline.

What dermatologists advise
The American Academy of Dermatology (AAD) lists tight ponytails, buns and cornrows among habits that damage hair, and advises wearing hair loosely pulled back.
For weaves and hair extensions, the AAD advises keeping them in for 2 or 3 months at most.
The AAD also advises keeping the scalp clean and alternating hairstyles, rather than always using the same tight style.

Put these into everyday words for your clients: "If it hurts, it is too tight. Tell me and I will redo it. Take these out by this date. After this style, give your hair a lighter style or a rest before we braid again." Write the agreed takedown date on her card and send her a WhatsApp reminder a week before.

Hygiene, Timing and Pricing Your Services

A skilled stylist still loses clients if her tools are dirty, her days run late or her prices do not cover her costs. This module gives you a between-client hygiene reset based on WHO and CDC guidance, a timing system for booking realistic days, and a pricing method that turns your service menu into steady income.
Hygiene between clients: the 15-minute reset
Clean and then disinfect tools and surfaces in the correct order
Mix a 0.1% bleach solution accurately from the strength on the label
Handle towels, capes and hair waste so nothing passes between clients
Wash hands correctly before and after every client

Combs, clips, towels and capes move from head to head all day. Without a routine, they can carry lice, fungal infections and bacteria from one client to the next. A clean salon is also something clients notice and talk about. This lesson builds a reset routine you do after every single client, which takes about 15 minutes once you are used to it, plus a deeper clean at the end of each day.
A person washing their hands
Clean hands at the start and end of every client are the cheapest protection in your salon.
Clean first, then disinfect

Cleaning removes hair, product and dirt with soap and water. Disinfecting kills germs that remain. You must clean first, because the World Health Organization (WHO) explains that surfaces must be cleaned with water and soap or a detergent to remove dirt before disinfection. A disinfectant poured over a comb full of hair and gel does very little.
Mixing a 0.1% bleach solution

WHO guidance for cleaning surfaces outside health facilities gives 0.1% sodium hypochlorite (household bleach) as a recommended concentration, which is 1 part of 5% household bleach to 49 parts of water. Bleach brands differ in strength, so read the percentage on your bottle. The general rule is: millilitres of bleach = 0.1 x total millilitres you want ÷ the bleach percentage on the label.
Worked example: mixing 2 litres of disinfectant
For example, Zainab in Jos wants 2 litres (2,000 ml) of 0.1% solution for her tool tray and surfaces.
With 5% bleach: 0.1 x 2,000 ÷ 5 = 40 ml of bleach.
Water: 2,000 minus 40 = 1,960 ml. Check: 40 is 1 part and 1,960 is 49 parts, because 40 x 49 = 1,960.
With a bleach labelled 3.5%: 0.1 x 2,000 ÷ 3.5 = about 57 ml of bleach, and 2,000 minus 57 = 1,943 ml of water.
She measures the bleach with a marked measuring cup kept only for bleach, pours it into the water, and labels the container "0.1% bleach, do not drink" with the date.
She mixes it in a well-ventilated place, wearing rubber gloves, and makes a fresh batch each working day.
Zainab has a correctly diluted solution for any bleach brand, instead of the common guess of "a little splash" that may be too weak to work or strong enough to irritate skin.
Bleach safety

WHO warns never to combine disinfectants such as bleach and ammonia, because mixtures can release dangerous gases. Never mix bleach with other cleaners. Wear rubber gloves, open windows, keep bleach away from children and food, and rinse tools in clean water after disinfecting. Bleach can damage metal, so use it on plastic combs and surfaces, and wash metal tools well with soap and water instead.
The reset after every client
Sweep up hair and put it in a covered bin. Do not leave it on the floor for the next client to walk through.
Remove used combs and clips to a "used" container. Never put them back on the tray.
Wash them in soapy water, scrub between the teeth with a small brush, and rinse.
Soak plastic tools in the 0.1% solution for the time recommended on your bleach label, then rinse in clean water and dry.
Wipe the chair, armrests, tray and mirror with soapy water, then with the bleach solution.
Put the used towel and cape in the laundry bag and take out fresh ones.
Wash your hands, then set out clean tools from the covered "clean" container.

First, density: how many strands grow on the scalp. Make a part at the crown, hairline, temples and nape, and see how much scalp shows. Temples are often thinnest.
Second, strand width. Hold a shed hair next to sewing thread. Thinner than the thread is fine hair, which breaks easily and needs less added weight.
Third, porosity: how water gets in and out. If sprayed water sits in droplets and dries slowly, porosity is low. If it soaks in and dries fast, it is high.
Fourth, elasticity. Do every check in daylight or with a phone torch, because dim light hides thin temples.

Step 2. Hold it firmly near the root, so you do not pull her scalp.
Step 3. Stretch it slowly and gently, then let go. Healthy hair springs back. Hair that snaps at once is brittle. Hair that stays stretched and gummy is weak.

When braids come out, clients are often shocked by the loose hair. Explain calmly. Shed hair cannot fall out while braided, and shedding 50 to 100 hairs a day is normal. A shed hair has a small white bulb.
Short pieces with no bulb are breakage. Write that on her card, especially if it comes from the edges.
Remove the shed hair with your fingers before you wet it, or the water mats it into knots.
Key points
Remember
Hot into cold, tested on your wrist
Section first; shampoo scalp, condition length
Blot, never rub; dry fully before braiding
Stretch with low heat or threading
Detangle damp, small sections, from the ends up

To remember. Test the water on your wrist. Wash in sections. Blot, never rub, and dry fully before braiding. Stretch with low heat or threading. Detangle damp hair in small sections, from the ends up.
With tender heads and children, take breaks and book more time instead of rushing.

Parting patterns
Clients judge a style first by its parts. Even parts also mean even weight, so no small section is strained.
In a square grid, the parts line up like a chessboard. Very neat when tied up, but lines of scalp show when the braids hang loose.
In brick-lay, each row is shifted by half a section, like bricks in a wall, so the scalp is covered better when the braids hang down. Choose the pattern with the client.
Step by step
Parting a full head
Every 2 rows, take a phone photo from behind and check sizes.
Start at the nape and clip the rest away
Divide the row into equal sections
Smooth each section with a little product
Finish the whole row before parting the next
Start at the nape. Draw the first row and clip all the hair above it away.
Divide the row into equal sections, using your fingers as a ruler.
Smooth each section with a little product. Mist dry hair lightly, or the parts go fuzzy.
Braid the whole row before you part the next one. Ask her to keep her chin level, and every 2 rows, check the back with a phone photo.
Worked example
Count before you quote
4 rows of 10 braids = 40 braids
4 shifted rows of 9 braids = 36 braids
Total: 76 braids
76 x 6 minutes = 456 minutes
For example, Aisha in Kano plans medium box braids in brick-lay, with 8 rows. Four rows hold 10 braids, which is 40. The four shifted rows hold 9 each, which is 36.
That is 76 braids. At her timed 6 minutes each, that is 456 minutes, about 7 hours 36 minutes of braiding. Now she can quote the time and buy the right hair.
Braid 2 or 3 stitches with her own hair only
Lay a thin, folded feed-in piece over the braid
Braid a few stitches, add the next piece
Stop adding at the agreed thickness
Check: no poking hairs, no tug at the root
Knotless braids look natural at the root because the weight builds slowly. Start with 2 or 3 stitches of her own hair only, firm but painless.
Lay a thin piece of extension hair, folded in half, over the braid so each half joins a side strand.
Braid 2 or 3 more stitches, then add the next piece the same way.
When the braid reaches the agreed thickness, braid to the end without adding more.
Run your fingers down it. No hairs poking out, and no tug at the root when she turns her head.

Safety
Sealing ends with hot water
Towel on her neck and shoulders. She leans away. Kettle on a stable surface, away from children.
Hold the cup well below her shoulders and dip only the ends. No open flame near her head.
Cool it under clean running water. Seek medical help for anything more than a small, mild burn.
Many stylists seal synthetic ends in hot water, and it burns quickly. Put a towel on her neck and shoulders, ask her to lean away, and keep the kettle away from children.
Hold the cup yourself, well below her shoulders, and dip only the ends. Never pour hot water over braids near her skin. Synthetic hair can catch fire, so never use a lighter near her head.
If skin is burned, cool it under clean running water, and seek medical help for anything more than a small, mild burn.
Traction alopecia
Signs the style is too tight
She winces or says it hurts
Skin lifts in little tents at the braid base
Redness around many bases
Bumps or soreness days later
Thinning temples over months
Traction alopecia is hair loss from repeated pulling. It often starts at the temples, and long-term pulling can make it permanent.
If she winces or says it hurts, stop and redo that section more loosely.
If the skin lifts in little tents, redo the braid. The scalp should lie flat.
Redness around many bases? Loosen the tightest rows before she leaves.
Bumps days later mean the tight braids should come out. Refer her if there is pus.
Thinning temples over months mean no tension at the hairline at all.
Every service
Tension check
Takedown date agreed
Run this check at the start, on every row, and before she leaves. Ask about past pain. Leave the hairline free and start cornrows thin. No tenting, no pain.
The course notes dermatologists advise extensions for 2 or 3 months at most, so agree a takedown date and remind her a week before.

Remember
Even parts mean even weight
Count braids and packs before you quote
Knotless and feed-ins add weight gradually
Hot water: towel, distance, ends only, no flame
If it hurts, it is too tight: redo it

To remember. Even parts mean even weight. Count braids and hair packs before you quote. Add extension weight gradually. Seal ends safely. And if it hurts, it is too tight. A child should never leave your chair in pain.

Why this matters
Skill alone does not keep clients
Dirty tools carry lice, fungus and bacteria
Guessed times make every client late
Copied prices may not cover your costs
A skilled stylist can still lose clients. Combs, clips and towels move from head to head, and without a routine they carry lice, fungal infections and bacteria.
Days run late when times are guessed instead of measured.
And a price copied from the salon down the road may not cover your own hair, products, fuel and time. This module fixes all three.
Worked example
Mixing 2 litres of 0.1% bleach
Never mix bleach with ammonia or any other cleaner.
Clean with soap and water first
5% bleach: 40 ml for 2,000 ml in total
Water: 2,000 minus 40 = 1,960 ml
Gloves on, window open, label and date it
Always clean first. Soap and water remove hair and gel. Disinfectant poured over a dirty comb does very little.
For example, Zainab in Jos wants 2 litres of 0.1% bleach solution. The rule is 0.1 times the total millilitres, divided by the percentage on the label. With 5% bleach, that is 40 ml of bleach.
The rest is water: 1,960 ml. That is 1 part bleach to 49 parts water. If your label shows a different strength, recalculate.
Mix it with rubber gloves on, in a ventilated place, away from children and food. Label it do not drink, with the date, and make it fresh each working day.
Never mix bleach with ammonia or other cleaners, because they can release dangerous gases.
After every client
The 15-minute reset
Sweep hair into a covered bin
Used combs and clips into the used box
Wash, scrub, soak plastic tools, rinse, dry
Wipe chair, tray and mirror
Fresh towel and cape for the next client
Wash hands for 40 to 60 seconds
After every single client, sweep the hair into a covered bin, and put used combs and clips straight into a used container. Never back on the tray.
Wash them in soapy water, scrub between the teeth, soak plastic tools in the bleach solution, then rinse and dry. Bleach damages metal, so wash metal tools with soap instead.
Wipe the chair, tray and mirror. One towel per client, so take a fresh towel and cape.
Then wash your hands for 40 to 60 seconds, and set out clean tools.
Timing
Book the whole service, not the braids
Log every stage for 10 services
Consultation, wash, stretch, braiding, finish
Braids x your minutes per braid
Add the 15-minute reset before the next booking
Late days come from guessing. For your next 10 services, write the start and end time of every stage, then work out your averages.
A service is consultation, prep, braiding and finishing.
For braiding, multiply the number of braids by your minutes per braid. For example, 76 braids at 6 minutes is 456 minutes.
Then add the reset before you book the next client. For example, Blessing in Owerri plans three Saturday bookings with resets and a 30-minute lunch, and finishes at 3 p.m. as she planned.

Money safety
About 30% when you buy hair. On a 13,000 naira style, she asks for 4,000 naira.
Open your own bank app and see the money in your balance. A screenshot or SMS is not proof.
If hair prices rise or a style takes longer, update the menu and tell regular clients first.
Ask for a deposit when you buy hair for a client. About 30% of 13,000 naira is 3,900, so Ifeoma asks for 4,000 naira, which covers the hair.
Fake transfer alerts and edited screenshots are a common trick. Before she leaves, open your own bank app and confirm the money is in your balance.
Review your prices every three months, and tell regular clients before a change. Fair changes are accepted. Surprise charges are not.

Price = materials + time + overhead + profit
Confirm every transfer in your own app
